passages.text: In 1764 a young Milanese aristocrat named Cesare Beccaria published a slim volume, On Crimes and Punishments, that would galvanize legal reformers across Europe and America. Writing in an era when torture was routinely used to extract confessions and when petty thefts could incur the death penalty, Beccaria argued that punishment is justified only insofar as it forestalls future crimes. ( ① ) Anything beyond that, he insisted, is gratuitous cruelty. ( ② ) His most enduring contention concerned how punishment deters. ( ③ ) A lenient penalty that follows a transgression swiftly and with near certainty, he reasoned, will dissuade offenders more effectively than a draconian penalty that they expect to evade. ( ④ ) Modern research has largely vindicated him: studies of deterrence suggest that people considering a crime respond far more to the probability of apprehension than to the length of the sentence they might receive. ( ⑤ ) This is why many criminologists contend that money spent on making arrests more probable may curtail crime more than money spent on keeping prisoners incarcerated longer.

Eyewitness testimony is among the most compelling kinds of evidence a jury can hear, yet memory is not a pristine recording that can simply be replayed. In a well-known study published in 1974, the psychologists Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed undergraduates short films of traffic collisions and then asked them how fast the cars had been going. ( ① ) The phrasing of the question varied subtly from group to group. ( ② ) Some students were asked how fast the cars were going when they hit each other; others heard the verbs smashed, collided, bumped, or contacted instead. Those who heard smashed gave the highest estimates, while those who heard contacted gave the lowest. ( ③ ) In a subsequent experiment, another cohort watched a similar film and answered the question with either smashed or hit. ( ④ ) A week later, all of them were asked whether they had seen any broken glass. ( ⑤ ) Students from the smashed group were more than twice as likely to say yes, although no glass had in fact been shattered. A single word, it seemed, had not merely skewed their answers but distorted what they remembered seeing.

Voice phishing, in which callers impersonate prosecutors, bank employees, or family members to dupe people into sending money, has cost victims in South Korea staggering sums, and the money rarely lingers where it is first sent. ( ① ) Criminal syndicates funnel illicit funds through bank accounts registered in other people's names, known in Korea as daepo accounts. ( ② ) Some of these accounts are bought from people in dire financial straits. ( ③ ) Others are relinquished by people who have been hoodwinked by bogus job advertisements promising lucrative work from home. ( ④ ) Many of these account holders later protest that they had no idea what their accounts would be used for. ( ⑤ ) Lending or selling one's account is itself a crime under Korean law, and those who do so can face criminal sanctions as well as restrictions on opening new accounts. Banks, for their part, can freeze accounts that are flagged in connection with fraud. Officials underscore one simple rule: no bona fide prosecutor or bank will ever ask a citizen to move money into a so-called safe account over the phone.

In March 1800, the Prussian naturalist Alexander von Humboldt arrived in the plains of what is now Venezuela, eager to scrutinize the electric eel, a fish capable of generating shocks of several hundred volts. ( ① ) Local guides proposed an unorthodox way of capturing them. ( ② ) They drove about thirty horses and mules into a murky pool where the eels lived. ( ③ ) The fish rose to the surface and pressed themselves against the animals' bellies, unleashing shock after shock. ( ④ ) Several horses collapsed, and at least two drowned. ( ⑤ ) After a while, however, the onslaught waned, and the depleted eels could be hauled from the water with little danger. For two centuries many scientists dismissed the story as an embellishment, since no one else had documented eels leaping from the water to attack. In 2016, however, the biologist Kenneth Catania reported that eels in his laboratory leapt from the water and pressed their chins against objects that approached them, delivering stronger shocks than they could underwater. Humboldt's horses, it seems, had been casualties of a genuine defensive behavior.

For most of the nineteenth century, police had no reliable way to prove that a particular person had been present at the scene of a crime. Witnesses could be mistaken or mendacious, and confessions were sometimes extracted under heavy duress.
(A) The investigator compared the print with impressions taken from the people involved. It matched the right thumb of the children's mother, Francisca Rojas, who then confessed. The case is often cited as the first crime solved by fingerprint evidence, and within a few years Argentina became one of the first countries to replace older identification methods with fingerprints.
(B) In the 1880s, scientists in Britain began to posit that the patterns of ridges on human fingertips were unique to each individual and remained immutable throughout life. Their ideas reached Juan Vucetich, a police official in Argentina, who devised his own system for classifying prints and began cataloguing the fingerprints of arrested men.
(C) In 1892, two young children were found dead in a village on the Argentine coast. Their mother accused a neighbor, who was arrested and interrogated harshly but denied everything. An investigator trained in Vucetich's methods then discerned a bloody thumbprint on a door frame of the house.

Salespeople have long maintained that the hardest part of persuasion is getting a customer to agree to anything at all. Once a small request has been accepted, the thinking goes, a larger one follows more easily. Door-to-door vendors, charity fundraisers, and political campaigners have all relied on this idea, though for a long time it rested on anecdote rather than evidence.
(A) Two weeks earlier, however, some of the residents had been visited by a different researcher, who asked them to display a small card, about three inches square, that exhorted people to be safe drivers. Nearly all of them had agreed to this innocuous request.
(B) In 1966 the psychologists Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser put this conviction to the test in California. A researcher asked homeowners whether they would allow a large, crudely lettered sign reading Drive Carefully to be placed on their front lawns. Fewer than one in five consented.
(C) Among these residents, more than three quarters agreed to the large sign. The researchers surmised that assenting to the first request had altered their self-perception: they had become, in their own eyes, the kind of citizens who champion worthy causes.

In January 2024, the company Neuralink implanted a wireless device in the brain of its first human volunteer, a man paralyzed below the shoulders after a diving accident. The device deciphers electrical signals from neurons involved in planning movement.
(A) Not everything went smoothly, however. Within weeks, many of the device's hair-thin threads retracted from the brain tissue, diminishing the number of signals the system could read, and engineers had to recalibrate the software so that the volunteer could keep using it.
(B) Such setbacks are not anomalous in a nascent field. University laboratories had enabled paralyzed patients to move cursors and robotic arms years earlier, but their systems relied on cumbersome equipment connected through the skull by cables. Several companies are now vying in the field, some with electrodes that rest on the surface of the brain instead of penetrating it. Still, turning a promising experiment into a dependable medical product remains a formidable task.
(C) Soon he was moving a cursor on a computer screen simply by thinking about moving his hand, and he played online chess for hours at a time. The results were widely hailed as a milestone.

On her first morning as a substitute teacher, Ms. Park was forewarned by the principal that the class she was taking over had driven away two exasperated teachers in a single term.
(A) She walked in, wrote her name on the board, and waited impassively. The din did not subside. So instead of bellowing, she took a stopwatch from her bag, set it on the desk, and announced that the class had just used up four minutes of its own lunch break. A few students snickered, but the laughter faded when she added that every further minute would come out of the same place.
(B) That afternoon the principal stopped her in the corridor to ask how she had survived. "I didn't have to do much," she replied. "They were too busy counting." She never divulged that the stopwatch had not been running at all.
(C) Thirty seconds later, the room was so hushed that she could hear the clock on the wall. A gangly boy in the front row raised his hand and asked how much of lunch they had left. "Exactly as much as you had yesterday," she said, "as long as we get through this lesson."

Sophocles' tragedy Antigone, first performed in Athens around 441 BCE, dramatizes a conflict that still vexes legal philosophers. After a civil war in which two brothers slay each other, the new king, Creon, decrees that one of them, a traitor in his eyes, must lie unburied. ① His sister Antigone defies the order and sprinkles earth over the corpse, insisting that the unwritten laws of the gods supersede any decree of a mortal ruler. ② Creon, for his part, argues that a city cannot endure if its citizens obey only the laws they personally approve of. ③ The theater of Dionysus, where such plays were staged, could seat many thousands of spectators on the slope below the Acropolis. ④ Neither character is unequivocally right, and the play punishes both: Antigone is condemned to death, and Creon loses his son and his wife. ⑤ Readers have since enlisted the play on both sides of the question of whether conscience can justify breaking the law, from dissidents under unjust regimes to defenders of public order.

In October 2024, the Tokyo Metropolitan Assembly passed what was described as Japan's first ordinance aimed specifically at customer harassment, known in Japanese by the abbreviated term kasuhara. ① The ordinance, which took effect in April 2025, prohibits customers from abusing workers through threats, insults, or exorbitant demands. ② It carries no penalties, but it urges businesses to devise guidelines for protecting their staff and makes clear that workers need not endure mistreatment as part of their jobs. ③ Surveys in Japan had found that a large share of service workers had been subjected to abuse from customers, sometimes including demands that they kneel in apology. ④ Japan is also known for its convenience stores, which sell everything from fresh rice balls to concert tickets around the clock. ⑤ Similar concerns have proliferated elsewhere; in South Korea, the emotional labor of call-center and retail workers has become a subject of public debate and legal protection. Critics of the ordinance worry that without penalties it will prove toothless, but supporters argue that its real purpose is to shift public expectations of how customers should behave.

Most hibernating mammals let their body temperature fall to just a few degrees above freezing. The arctic ground squirrel of Alaska and northern Canada goes much further. ① During hibernation, which can last up to eight months, its core temperature plummets below zero degrees Celsius, reaching nearly minus three degrees, yet its blood does not freeze. ② The phenomenon, documented by the physiologist Brian Barnes in 1989, is known as supercooling: in the absence of ice crystals to seed it, the fluid remains liquid well below its normal freezing point. ③ Remarkably, the squirrel does not stay in this state throughout the winter but rouses itself every few weeks, shivering vigorously to rewarm its body for about a day before plunging back into torpor. ④ Arctic summers, by contrast, are brief, and the tundra where the squirrels burrow is carpeted with wildflowers for only a few weeks each year. ⑤ These periodic arousals consume most of the energy it expends all winter, and scientists still debate why they are necessary. Medical researchers are scrutinizing the animal closely, hoping that its tolerance of extreme cold and reduced blood flow might suggest ways to protect human organs during surgery or after strokes.

In the early 1960s, the Yale psychologist Stanley Milgram asked volunteers to take part in what they believed was a study of learning. Each volunteer was instructed to administer electric shocks of increasing strength to a learner in another room whenever he made a mistake. ① The shocks were not real, and the learner was an actor who protested, cried out, and eventually fell silent. ② About two thirds of the volunteers in the best-known version continued to the highest level when the experimenter calmly insisted that they go on. ③ Milgram concluded that ordinary people will perpetrate harmful acts when instructed by an authority they regard as legitimate. ④ Later scholars, however, have impugned this interpretation, noting that many participants doubted the shocks were real and that obedience plummeted when the experimenter's authority seemed more tenuous. ⑤ Yale, founded in 1701, is one of the oldest universities in the United States. The experiments also prompted stricter ethical rules for research, since many volunteers had left the laboratory deeply traumatized.

On November 19, 1863, a throng of about fifteen thousand gathered at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, to dedicate a cemetery for soldiers killed in the battle fought there that July. The main speaker was Edward Everett, a former secretary of state and one of the most illustrious orators in the country, who spoke for about two hours, recounting the battle in meticulous detail. President Abraham Lincoln, invited almost as an afterthought to offer a few appropriate remarks, then rose and spoke for roughly two minutes. His address contained about 270 words. Newspaper verdicts diverged largely along partisan lines. Everett, however, wrote to the president the next day, saying that he would be glad if he had come as near to the central idea of the occasion in two hours as Lincoln had in two minutes. Today Everett's speech is almost forgotten, while Lincoln's is memorized by schoolchildren and inscribed in stone on the wall of his memorial in Washington. Its brevity, far from diminishing it, gave each sentence a gravity that a longer speech could not have carried.

For many years, stalking in South Korea was treated as a minor offense, punishable at most by a small fine under a law covering misdemeanors such as littering. Victims who reported being shadowed or inundated with unwanted messages were often told that the police could do little until something graver happened. A spate of cases in which stalking culminated in violence transformed public opinion, and in 2021 a law specifically punishing stalking took effect. Even that law soon drew censure. It originally allowed prosecution to be dropped if the victim did not wish to pursue it, a provision that exposed victims to coercion from the very people they feared. In 2023 lawmakers revised the law, removing this provision and allowing courts to order electronic monitoring of suspects during investigations, a measure that took effect the following year. The changes reflect a broader shift in how the offense is understood: stalking is no longer seen as an awkward surfeit of romantic ardor but as ____.

Witnesses to armed robberies often give elaborate descriptions of the weapon but strikingly hazy accounts of the robber's face. Psychologists call this the weapon focus effect. In laboratory studies, participants watch a short scene in which a man approaches a cashier holding either a gun or an ordinary object such as a checkbook. Those who see the gun spend more time fixating on it and are later less accurate at picking out the man from a set of photographs. The intuitive explanation is fear: a weapon signals danger, and a frightened mind narrows its attention to the source of the threat. Yet later research muddied this account. Studies found that a bizarre but harmless object, one that simply did not belong in the scene, could draw the eyes in much the same way. The weapon, it seems, captures attention not only because it is dangerous but because ____. For investigators, the lesson is that a witness's confident description of a gun says little about the reliability of her identification of the person holding it.

In 1999 the psychologists Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris asked volunteers to watch a short video of two teams passing basketballs and to count the passes made by the players in white. About halfway through, a person in a gorilla suit sauntered into the middle of the scene, faced the camera, thumped its chest, and walked off. Roughly half of the viewers were utterly oblivious to it, and some, when shown the video again, refused to believe it was the same recording. The phenomenon, known as inattentional blindness, is not a symptom of negligence or poor eyesight. It reflects the way attention works: when we concentrate on one task, the brain filters out much of what is irrelevant to it, even when that material appears in plain view. The finding has unsettling implications for anyone who relies on what witnesses report. A driver who insists that a cyclist came out of nowhere may be recounting candidly what he experienced. Looking directly at something, in other words, ____.

In June 1925, a twenty-three-year-old German physicist named Werner Heisenberg, afflicted by a severe bout of hay fever, retreated to Helgoland, a rocky island in the North Sea almost free of pollen. There, working late into the night, he decided to ____. Instead of picturing electrons circling the nucleus in tidy orbits that no experiment could ever detect, he would describe atoms using only quantities that could actually be measured, such as the frequencies of the light they gave off. The paper he wrote on his return is often heralded as the birth of quantum mechanics, and to mark its centenary the United Nations declared 2025 the International Year of Quantum Science and Technology. The theory that grew from it is famously counterintuitive: particles behave in some experiments like waves, and certain pairs of properties cannot both be known precisely at the same time. Yet it is also among the most rigorously tested theories in science, and it undergirds technologies ranging from lasers to the transistors inside every phone.

Ernest Hemingway likened good writing to an iceberg: only a small part should show above the surface, while the rest remains hidden below. In his 1932 book on bullfighting, Death in the Afternoon, he argued that a writer who truly knows his subject can omit things, and that the reader, if the writing is honest, will feel those things as strongly as if they had been stated. His short story Hills Like White Elephants, published in 1927, shows the method at work. A man and a woman wait for a train at a small Spanish station, sipping beer and chatting about the scenery and about an operation that the man insists is simple. The nature of the operation is never named, nor does either character state directly what he or she feels. Yet by the end, most readers intuit that the relationship is disintegrating. The technique demands trust in both directions: the writer must trust the reader to notice, and the reader must trust that the silences are deliberate. Hemingway believed that ____.

My aunt ran a small photo studio on the second floor of a building near the market, and on Saturdays I was allowed to help. Most customers came for passport pictures, which she took with a speed and confidence that seemed (A) [effortless / hesitant]: a quick adjustment of the chin, a word about the eyes, a single click. Wedding portraits and family photographs were different. For those she might spend an hour rearranging a grandmother's shawl or waiting for a fidgety toddler to (B) [settle / unsettle]. Once I asked why she did not simply take dozens of pictures and pick the best. She said that a camera can record a face in an instant, but it cannot make a person feel at ease; that part was her job, and it could not be hurried. Years later, when I stumbled upon a box of her old prints, I noticed that the people in them looked (C) [stiff / relaxed] in a way that people in my own phone photos rarely do. I had always thought her slowness was a quirk of her generation. Looking at those faces, I understood it had been a skill.

Most students assume that answering questions before studying a topic is futile, since they are bound to get the answers wrong. Research suggests otherwise. In a series of experiments, learners who first tried to guess the answers to questions about a passage, and then read it, later (A) [remembered / forgot] the material better than learners who simply spent the same amount of time reading. The benefit appeared even though nearly all of the initial guesses were erroneous. Psychologists proffer several explanations. An unsuccessful attempt may pique learners' curiosity about the right answer, so that they read with greater (B) [attention / indifference]. It may also reveal what they do not yet know, dispelling the common illusion that a passage they have skimmed is already understood. The wrong guesses themselves rarely (C) [persist / desist], provided that learners receive the correct answers soon afterward. For teachers, the lesson is that a short quiz at the start of a lesson need not be graded to be useful; its purpose is not to measure what students know but to prepare them to learn.

The high seas, the vast expanses of ocean beyond any country's jurisdiction, cover nearly half of the planet's surface, yet for decades they were governed by a patchwork of fragmented rules that left most of them unprotected. In January 2026 a new international treaty, commonly called the High Seas Treaty, entered into force after more than sixty countries had ratified it. Adopted at the United Nations in 2023 after nearly two decades of arduous negotiation, the agreement establishes, for the first time, a mechanism for creating marine protected areas in international waters. It also requires assessments of the environmental impact of activities planned there and sets rules for sharing the benefits of marine genetic resources, such as compounds from deep-sea organisms that may yield new medicines. Supporters regard the treaty as indispensable to the widely endorsed goal of protecting thirty percent of the ocean by 2030. Skeptics caution that it lacks a strong enforcement mechanism and that some major maritime powers have not ratified it. Even so, it marks a significant shift: the open ocean is no longer treated simply as a frontier to be exploited, but as a shared inheritance to be managed.

The Roman philosopher Seneca wrote a long treatise on anger in the first century, and his advice remains surprisingly pragmatic. Anger, he argued, is the most pernicious of the passions because it disguises itself as justice. The angry person feels not that he is losing control but that he is finally seeing clearly, and so he acts in ways he would never condone in a calmer moment. Seneca rejected the view, held by some philosophers of his time, that anger could be harnessed for good purposes; in his eyes it was a servant that quickly became a master. His most useful remedy was delay. The first surge of anger, he observed, is almost impossible to stifle, but no one is obliged to act on it immediately. A person who waits allows judgment to catch up with feeling, and many offenses that seemed intolerable in the moment turn out, on reflection, to be trivial or misunderstood. He also advocated reviewing one's day each evening and asking where one had been unreasonable. The goal was not to feel nothing but to give reason time to speak.

Kim Jeong-ho, a mapmaker of the late Joseon period, completed the Daedongyeojido, a map of the Korean Peninsula, in 1861. Remarkably little is known about his life; even the years of his birth and death are uncertain. The map was printed from carved woodblocks, which allowed copies to be made far more cheaply than by hand. It was divided into twenty-two sections, each folded like the pages of a book, so that a traveler could carry only the parts needed for a particular journey. When all of the sections are laid out together, the map stands more than six meters tall. Rivers are drawn with double lines where boats could travel on them and with single lines where they could not, and roads are marked with small ticks every ten ri, letting users gauge distances at a glance. A popular legend claims that the authorities, alarmed that the map disclosed national secrets, imprisoned Kim and destroyed his woodblocks. Historians now regard this tale as unfounded, and some of the original woodblocks survive in the National Museum of Korea.

Shortly after noon on April 28, 2025, the electricity supply across almost all of Spain and Portugal collapsed within a matter of seconds. Trains stalled between stations, traffic lights went dark, and many people lost mobile phone service as the backup batteries at transmission sites ran down. Hospitals switched to their own generators. Power began to return within hours, and by the following morning supply had been restored almost everywhere. The blackout prompted an acrimonious debate about its causes. Because solar power was supplying a large share of Spain's electricity at that moment, some pundits blamed renewable energy, arguing that grids dominated by solar panels lack the stabilizing inertia provided by the heavy spinning turbines of conventional power plants. Official investigations, however, pointed to a more intricate chain of events involving problems in controlling voltage, and officials ruled out a cyberattack. Engineers note that the episode was less a verdict on any single source of energy than a reminder that grids undergoing rapid transformation need new tools to keep them stable.

For thirty years Mr. Gu ran a cramped bicycle repair shop beside the elementary school, and the children regarded him with a mixture of awe and terror. He was gruff, he charged exactly what the repair was worth, and he refused to fix anything a child had broken through sheer carelessness until the child could explain what had gone wrong. To Mr. Gu, mending a bicycle was less a trade than an act of ____, and he expected the same patience from his young customers. One autumn a boy named Taeho arrived with a bicycle so mangled that most adults would have advised him to buy a new one. The boy had no money; the bicycle had belonged to his late grandfather. Mr. Gu told Taeho to come back every afternoon after school. For six weeks the boy sat on an upturned crate, handing over wrenches, straightening spokes, and learning the names of parts he had never noticed. When the bicycle finally rolled out of the shop, gleaming, Taeho asked how much he owed. Mr. Gu shook his head. The bill, he said, had already been paid in afternoons. Years later, Taeho would say that the shop had taught him something no classroom had: that some things are worth repairing because of what they carry, not what they cost.

Niccolo Machiavelli's The Prince, written in 1513 after he had been dismissed from the government of Florence, poses a question that rulers had rarely heard put so bluntly: is it better to be loved or feared? Machiavelli's answer is that it would be best to be both, but since the two rarely go together, it is safer to be feared. Love, he argues, depends on the goodwill of others, which can evaporate the moment their interests change; fear depends on the ruler himself, who can sustain it through the prospect of punishment. Yet the passage is often quoted without its crucial caveat. Machiavelli insists that a prince must shun being hated, and he warns that the surest way to provoke hatred is to confiscate the property of his subjects or to dishonor their families. Fear, in his account, is useful only when it is ____; a ruler must be able to calibrate it and his subjects to anticipate its limits. A ruler who terrifies people at random does not earn obedience; he invites conspiracy. Read carefully, the book is less a celebration of cruelty than a cold calculation of what keeps power stable.

In September 1984, the British geneticist Alec Jeffreys was investigating the inheritance of hereditary disorders at the University of Leicester when he spotted an anomaly on an X-ray film. ( ① ) Certain stretches of DNA, duplicated many times over, varied so drastically in length between individuals that the pattern they generated resembled a bar code peculiar to each person. ( ② ) He swiftly realized that the technique could distinguish individuals from minute samples of blood or other biological material. ( ③ ) Its first momentous test came in 1986, when police investigating the murders of two adolescent girls in nearby villages enlisted his help. ( ④ ) A young man had already confessed to one of the killings, yet the DNA demonstrated that he could not have committed either. ( ⑤ ) Police then asked thousands of local men to furnish samples, and the real culprit, Colin Pitchfork, was eventually apprehended after a colleague was overheard admitting that he had given a sample in Pitchfork's place. The case thus also yielded one of the first convictions based on DNA evidence. Today, DNA databases help solve crimes around the world, although they also raise thorny questions about privacy.

Thomas Hobbes published Leviathan in 1651, shortly after the English Civil War had shown him how precarious political order could be. ( ① ) He invited his readers to envisage human life without any government at all, a condition he called the state of nature. ( ② ) In such a world, he argued, people would be roughly equal in their capacity to harm one another, since even the feeblest could kill the strongest by cunning or in alliance with others. ( ③ ) Each person would therefore have reason to dread everyone else and to strike preemptively. ( ④ ) There would be no husbandry, no commerce, and no science, because no one could be assured of reaping the fruits of his labor. ( ⑤ ) Life, in his most famous phrase, would be solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. To escape this predicament, people would consent to surrender their power to a sovereign formidable enough to keep the peace. Critics have countered that Hobbes's sovereign could itself become an instrument of tyranny, but his central claim, that security is the paramount purpose of government, still underpins debates about the state.

In the summer of 2024, South Korea was shaken by reports that sexually explicit images of women, fabricated by grafting their faces onto other bodies with artificial intelligence, were proliferating in online chat rooms. Many of the victims were university students, teachers, and even schoolgirls. ( ① ) Many of the perpetrators sharing the images, moreover, turned out to be teenagers themselves. ( ② ) The public backlash was swift and vociferous. ( ③ ) Within weeks, the National Assembly amended the law on sexual crimes so that knowingly possessing, purchasing, or viewing such material became a crime punishable by up to three years in prison. ( ④ ) The amendment also stiffened the maximum sentence for producing or distributing it. ( ⑤ ) Supporters argued that a counterfeit image can devastate a real person's life as surely as a genuine photograph, while some jurists questioned how prosecutors would prove that a person knew an image was illicit. Schools, meanwhile, began admonishing students that creating such images, even as a prank, is a grave crime rather than an innocuous joke.

Why do people sometimes behave in a crowd in ways they would never countenance alone? Psychologists use the term deindividuation for the erosion of self-awareness that can occur when people feel anonymous and engulfed by a group. ( ① ) A study conducted on Halloween in the 1970s offered a memorable illustration. ( ② ) Researchers arranged for costumed children who came trick-or-treating at certain homes in Seattle to be greeted by a woman who invited them to take a single piece of candy from a bowl and then left the room. ( ③ ) Some children were asked their names and addresses before she departed; others remained anonymous behind their masks. ( ④ ) Children who were anonymous and in groups pilfered extra candy far more often than children who were alone and had disclosed their names. ( ⑤ ) Being identifiable, it seems, keeps people tethered to their customary standards. The finding is often invoked in debates about anonymity, from masked crowds at demonstrations to the comment sections of the internet, though researchers caution that anonymity can also embolden people to act more magnanimously.

In 1401, King Taejong of Joseon decreed that a large drum be hung outside the royal palace in Hanyang. Any subject with a grievance that local officials had failed to redress could, in principle, strike it to bring the complaint directly to the king's attention.
(A) Partly because of these obstacles, the system fell into disuse and was abolished and reinstated several times over the following centuries. Later monarchs experimented with other channels, such as permitting commoners to petition by striking a gong when the king passed in a procession, a practice that brought the ruler's ear somewhat closer to the streets.
(B) The drum became known as the sinmungo, and its very existence was intended as a political statement. A ruler who invited complaints was proclaiming that injustice anywhere in the kingdom concerned him personally, a claim rooted in the Confucian ideal of a monarch who cares for his people as a father cares for his children.
(C) In practice, however, the drum seldom served the people it was ostensibly meant for. Stringent regulations required petitioners first to exhaust every lower level of appeal, and the palace was remote from most villages. Records intimate that it was used mostly by officials and residents of the capital, sometimes for matters as private as inheritance disputes.

In March 2025, schools in South Korea began using digital textbooks equipped with artificial intelligence in subjects such as English and mathematics. The government promised that the software would tailor itself to each student, offering easier problems to those who floundered and more demanding ones to those who were ahead.
(A) Within months, the National Assembly amended the textbooks' legal status, reclassifying them as supplementary learning materials. Schools could still use them, but they were no longer obliged to, and the decision was left to each school.
(B) Teachers and parents, however, voiced misgivings from the outset. Some worried about the cost and the training required, others about the hours children would squander staring at screens, and still others about how students' personal data would be stored and safeguarded.
(C) The episode epitomizes a recurring pattern in educational technology. Novel tools often arrive with grandiose promises, but their value depends less on the software itself than on whether teachers have the time and support to wield it well. A tablet cannot compensate for a curriculum that nobody has had time to plan.

Almost every living thing, from bacteria to human beings, follows an internal rhythm of roughly twenty-four hours. This circadian clock signals to the body when to sleep, when to release certain hormones, and when to digest food.
(A) Working with fruit flies, three American scientists, Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young, isolated a gene that governs this rhythm. They showed that the protein it encodes accumulates in cells during the night and degrades during the day, forming a self-regulating loop. In 2017 they received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this work.
(B) Their discovery has tangible consequences. When the internal clock falls out of step with the outside world, as it does during jet lag or prolonged night-shift work, people may suffer not only fatigue but, over time, a heightened risk of various ailments.
(C) For a long time, however, no one knew how such a clock could operate at the level of individual cells. Scientists had observed as early as the eighteenth century that some plants open and close their leaves on a daily cycle even when kept in constant darkness, but the mechanism remained an enigma.

It was nearly midnight when the last passenger of Mr. Choi's shift climbed out of his taxi in front of a maternity hospital, thanked him twice, and scurried through the glass doors without looking back.
(A) The call came at six in the morning. The passenger, whose wife had given birth in the small hours, had found the note at the front desk and had not even realized the bag was missing. When Mr. Choi handed it over in the hospital lobby, the man tried to force money on him, and when he refused, pressed a box of rice cakes into his hands instead.
(B) He promptly drove back to the hospital, but without a name the receptionist on duty could do little. Mr. Choi left his phone number along with a description of the bag and, somewhat reluctantly, went home to sleep.
(C) Only when he stopped for fuel twenty minutes later did he notice a small leather bag on the back seat. Inside were a wallet, a set of keys, and a tiny knitted cap still wrapped in tissue paper.

In 1963, Ernesto Miranda was arrested in Phoenix, Arizona, and after two hours of police interrogation signed a confession. ① He had never been informed that he had the right to remain silent or to have a lawyer present. ② In 1966 the United States Supreme Court overturned his conviction, ruling that statements obtained during custodial questioning were inadmissible unless suspects had first been apprised of these rights. ③ The warning that resulted, beginning with the words you have the right to remain silent, has since become familiar to viewers around the world through films and television dramas. ④ Miranda himself was killed in 1976 in a fight at a bar in Phoenix, and the man arrested for the stabbing was reportedly read the very warning that bore his name. ⑤ Police organizations initially predicted that the ruling would make confessions scarce and crimes insoluble, but research in the following decades found that most suspects still elected to talk. Miranda had in fact been retried using other evidence and convicted again, a telling reminder that the decision safeguarded a procedure rather than any particular defendant.

Parents have always flaunted photographs of their children, but the internet has transformed the audience from a handful of relatives into potentially millions of strangers. The habit of sharing children's images online has even acquired its own name: sharenting. ① In February 2024, France adopted a law stating explicitly that parents must protect their children's right to their own image and must take the child's privacy into account. ② Under the law, if parents are at odds over posting a child's photographs, a judge can prohibit one of them from doing so without the other's consent. ③ In especially egregious cases, a court can even transfer the right to manage a child's image to a third party. ④ In 2023, French lawmakers had also voted to require parental consent before children under fifteen could open social media accounts of their own. ⑤ Supporters point out that photographs posted today may haunt children into adulthood, revealing their whereabouts, mortifying them in front of future classmates, or being misappropriated by strangers. Skeptics doubt that the law will be easy to enforce, but its proponents say its main purpose is to change parents' habits rather than to fill courtrooms.

Homing pigeons released hundreds of kilometers from their lofts can find their way back, a skill that humans exploited for thousands of years to convey messages. How they accomplish this feat has perplexed scientists for just as long. ① Experiments suggest that pigeons use the position of the sun as a compass, compensating for the time of day with their internal clocks. ② When the sky is overcast, they appear to rely on the earth's magnetic field instead. ③ Near home, they also discern familiar landmarks such as highways, rivers, and coastlines, and some studies indicate that they follow roads even when a straighter route is available. ④ Several experiments further suggest that odors carried on the wind contribute to their orientation. ⑤ Pigeons are also omnipresent in city squares, where many residents regard them as a nuisance because of the mess they leave on buildings and statues. No single cue explains the achievement; rather, the birds seem to integrate several sources of information, switching between them as circumstances change.

In August 1971, the psychologist Philip Zimbardo recruited undergraduates to play guards and prisoners in a mock prison built in the basement of a building at Stanford University. ① The study was planned to last two weeks but was halted after six days, reportedly because some guards had become sadistic and several prisoners displayed signs of acute distress. ② For decades, the experiment was taught as proof that ordinary people thrust into a powerful role will quickly abuse it. ③ Later investigations of recordings and archives, however, revealed that the guards had been goaded by the researchers to act tough, and some participants confessed they had been performing the parts they surmised were expected of them. ④ Zimbardo himself went on to a distinguished career and was elected president of the American Psychological Association in 2002. ⑤ Many psychologists now argue that the study reveals less about the power of situations than about the influence of leaders who tell people what a role requires. It remains a riveting story, but it is a flimsy foundation for sweeping conclusions about human nature.

Victor Hugo's Les Miserables, published in 1862, follows Jean Valjean, a man imprisoned for nineteen years for stealing bread and later attempting to escape, who is transformed by an unexpected act of clemency from a bishop and spends the rest of his life doing good under an assumed name. Pursuing him for decades is Javert, a police inspector who is not a villain in any ordinary sense. He is scrupulously upright, incorruptible, and utterly devoted to the law, which he regards as the only bulwark between society and chaos. For Javert, a person who has once broken the law remains a criminal forever; repentance is irrelevant. The crisis comes when Valjean, given the chance to kill his pursuer, sets him free instead. Javert later finds himself in a position to arrest Valjean and cannot bring himself to do it. Unable to reconcile his rigid sense of duty with the mercy he has received and now shown, he is destroyed by the contradiction. Hugo's point is not that law is worthless but that law without mercy cannot account for the capacity of human beings to change.

When investigators seize a phone or a laptop, the cardinal and inviolable rule of digital forensics is to avoid altering anything on it. Merely switching a computer on can modify thousands of files, updating the dates on which they were last opened and overwriting data that might otherwise have been retrieved. Examiners therefore usually work not on the original device but on an exact replica of its storage, made with equipment that prevents anything from being written back to the original. To verify that the copy is faithful, they calculate a hash value, a long string of characters generated from the data by a mathematical formula. Changing even a single character in the data yields a completely different hash, so identical values before and after an examination demonstrate that nothing has been tampered with. Every person who handles the evidence is documented in a log known as the chain of custody. These procedures may seem tedious and pedantic, but in court the crucial question is often not only what a device contains but ____.

In the third century BCE, as rival states in China vied for supremacy, the philosopher Han Feizi repudiated the Confucian belief that rulers could govern through moral example. People, he argued, are moved chiefly by self-interest: they covet rewards and shun punishment. A shrewd ruler should therefore not rely on the virtue of his ministers or subjects but on explicit laws, publicly proclaimed and applied without exception, with munificent rewards for those who obey and severe penalties for those who do not. The law, in his celebrated metaphor, does not bend to the noble any more than a carpenter's measuring line bends around a crooked piece of wood. The state of Qin adopted ideas of this kind and went on to unify China in 221 BCE. Yet the Qin dynasty disintegrated within fifteen years, and later historians blamed its harshness for fomenting rebellion. Han Feizi's legacy is thus double-edged: his insistence that the law ____ anticipated a principle modern societies cherish, while his faith in draconian punishment has largely been rejected.

In 1956 the psychologist George Miller published a paper with a whimsical title, The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two. Surveying a range of experiments, he observed that people could hold about seven items, such as digits or words, in immediate memory before they began to falter. The number became one of the most widely cited findings in psychology, invoked to justify everything from the length of telephone numbers to the number of options on a menu. Subsequent research, however, suggested that Miller's estimate was too generous. People remember long strings of digits partly by grouping them into chunks, as when a phone number is split into sections, and when such grouping is precluded, the true capacity appears closer to four items. Designers who assume that users can juggle seven separate pieces of information may therefore be demanding far too much of them. The psychologist Nelson Cowan, who scrutinized this evidence in 2001, argued that ____.

In 2024 the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences went to Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson, and James Robinson for research on how institutions shape the prosperity of nations. One of their favorite illustrations is the city of Nogales, which is bisected by the border between the United States and Mexico. The inhabitants on both sides share ancestors, a climate, and much of their culture, yet residents of the northern half are on average far more affluent, healthier, and better served by public services. The yawning disparity, the economists contend, lies not in geography or culture but in rules: on one side, institutions that protect property, enforce contracts, and give citizens a voice in government; on the other, institutions that have historically served narrower interests. Their historical research traced such differences back to the colonial era, when Europeans built very different institutions depending on whether they intended to settle in a territory or merely plunder its resources. The lesson they draw is that ____. Detractors argue that the theory underplays other factors, but few dispute that rules matter enormously.

On April 26, 1937, during the Spanish Civil War, German and Italian aircraft supporting General Franco bombed the Basque town of Guernica on a bustling market day, razing much of the town and killing many civilians. Pablo Picasso, living in Paris, had been commissioned to paint a mural for the Spanish pavilion at the forthcoming World's Fair. He discarded his earlier plans and, within about five weeks, produced an immense canvas in black, white, and gray. It contains no airplanes and no bombs. Instead, it depicts a shrieking mother cradling a dead child, an anguished horse, a slain soldier, and a woman leaning from a window with a lamp. By refusing to depict the event literally, Picasso created a picture that ____. Picasso stipulated that the painting should not go to Spain until democracy had been restored there, and it arrived in Madrid only in 1981, several years after Franco's death. It now hangs in a museum in the capital, where crowds still congregate before it in a silence that few paintings command.

Our neighbor Mrs. Han kept four beehives at the bottom of her garden, and for most of my childhood I was (A) [terrified / fond] of them. Every summer I would cross the street rather than walk past her fence, convinced that the bees were lying in wait for me. In the fourth grade, she finally coaxed me into watching her open a hive, and to my astonishment she wore no gloves. She moved unhurriedly, she explained, because bees react to abrupt movements, and she never opened a hive on a cold or stormy day, when the colony was (B) [calm / irritable]. I watched her lift a frame laden with honey while dozens of bees ambled across her bare wrists, and not one of them stung her. That autumn she gave me a jar with my name written on the lid. I still cannot profess to love insects, but I learned something that afternoon that has served me in many situations since: much of what we fear becomes (C) [manageable / unmanageable] once we understand what provokes it.

Students are often counseled to rewrite their notes in order to remember them. Research by psychologists at the University of Waterloo suggests that drawing may work even better. In a series of experiments, participants were given a list of simple words, such as apple, and asked either to write each word out repeatedly or to sketch a quick picture of it within the same amount of time. On a surprise test afterward, those who had illustrated the words (A) [retained / detained] substantially more of them, and the advantage persisted even among participants who considered themselves inept at drawing. The quality of the pictures appeared immaterial. The researchers suggest that drawing compels learners to (B) [combine / separate] several kinds of processing at once: pondering what a word means, imagining its appearance, and moving the hand to create it. Writing a word repeatedly, by contrast, can be done almost (C) [mechanically / thoughtfully], with scant attention to its meaning. The findings do not imply that every lesson should become an art class, but they suggest that even crude sketches can make information stick.

The 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson, and Omar Yaghi for developing metal-organic frameworks. These materials are assembled from metal ions linked by long organic molecules, forming crystals riddled with regularly shaped cavities. The cavities are so numerous that a few grams of some frameworks contain an internal surface area roughly the size of a football field. Because chemists can choose the building blocks, they can tailor frameworks whose pores capture particular molecules. Researchers have devised versions that harvest water vapor from desert air, trap carbon dioxide from industrial exhaust, store volatile gases securely, and decompose toxic substances. Robson built the first rudimentary structures in the late 1980s, but they were fragile and prone to collapse; the work of Kitagawa and Yaghi in the 1990s showed that they could be made robust and even flexible. Many applications remain at an early stage, and manufacturing the materials cheaply at scale is still a formidable challenge. Nevertheless, the prize recognized an entirely new way of designing matter, one in which empty space itself becomes the most valuable ingredient.

Anton Chekhov is credited with a piece of advice that writers still repeat: if a gun hangs on the wall in the first act of a play, it must be discharged by the last. The principle is notoriously misconstrued as a rule about guns or about foreshadowing alone. Its deeper point concerns economy. Every detail in a story makes a tacit and binding promise to the audience that it matters, and an audience that has been plied with dozens of details will squander its attention trying to remember them all. A detail that is never used therefore does not merely occupy space; it misleads. Chekhov's own stories exemplify this austere discipline. They are often short, unhurried, and deceptively plain, yet almost nothing in them is idle. Modern editors apply the same logic when they urge writers to excise scenes that are beautifully written but serve no purpose, however painful the cut may be. The test is not whether a passage is good in isolation but whether the story would lose anything without it.

In 1967 the British philosopher Philippa Foot described a puzzle that would become one of the most debated in moral philosophy. A runaway tram is hurtling toward five workers on the track, and its driver can steer onto a side track where it will kill one worker instead. Most people say that steering is permissible. Yet in a variation later developed by the American philosopher Judith Jarvis Thomson, who coined the name trolley problem, the only way to save the five is to push a large man off a footbridge into the tram's path. Although the arithmetic is identical, most people say this is wrong. Philosophers have spent decades striving to explain the discrepancy, pointing to distinctions between killing and letting die or between harming someone as a means and harming someone as a side effect. The puzzle gained fresh urgency with the development of self-driving cars. A 2018 online experiment called the Moral Machine amassed millions of decisions from people in more than two hundred countries and territories about whom a car should spare in an unavoidable crash, revealing both shared intuitions and striking cultural differences.

In December 2024, South Korea officially became a super-aged society, with people aged sixty-five or older making up more than a fifth of the population. One consequence is conspicuous on the roads. The number of older drivers has swelled steadily, and so has the share of traffic accidents in which they are at fault. Many local governments now encourage older residents to relinquish their licenses voluntarily, offering inducements such as prepaid transportation cards. Drivers aged seventy-five or older must also renew their licenses more frequently than younger drivers and complete a safety course that includes a test of cognitive ability. Yet the policy debate is far from tidy. Age alone is a crude and unreliable predictor of driving skill, and many older people in rural areas, where buses are sparse, depend on their cars to reach hospitals and markets. Revoking a license can leave them isolated. Some specialists therefore favor tests that measure actual driving ability rather than rigid age limits, along with better public transportation and, eventually, vehicles that can assist or even replace the driver.

For two years I worked the night shift at a convenience store across from a hospital, and the customers who came after midnight were seldom in a hurry to leave. There were nurses buying instant noodles at the end of grueling shifts, cabbies nursing canned coffee by the window, and an elderly man who arrived every night at two and bought a single newspaper, although the morning edition had not yet come out and he always had to settle for yesterday's. For months I presumed he was befuddled. One night I ventured, as gently as I could, that the new paper would arrive at five. He smiled wistfully and said he knew. His wife was in the hospital across the street, he explained, and he could not sleep at home, and buying a newspaper gave him a reason to walk somewhere and speak to someone. What he was really purchasing every night, I came to see, was ____. After that I set the crossword page aside for him, and on quiet nights we argued cheerfully over the answers until the delivery truck arrived. I have forgotten most of the prices I memorized in that job, but I have never forgotten that for some people, a shop at night is less a place to buy things than a place to be.

In George Orwell's novel Nineteen Eighty-Four, published in 1949, the ruling Party is fashioning a new language called Newspeak. Unlike every other language, it is designed to dwindle each year. Words are abolished outright or stripped of their unwanted meanings, so that free, for example, can still describe a field free of weeds but no longer refers to political liberty. The aim, as one character explains with unsettling enthusiasm, is to make certain thoughts literally impossible, since a person cannot think clearly about what he has no words for. Orwell's appendix on Newspeak reads like a dry linguistic report, which renders it all the more chilling. Modern linguists generally doubt that language constrains thought as completely as the novel imagines; people routinely apprehend ideas before they find names for them. Yet Orwell's warning concerns something subtler than grammar. Political language, he had argued in an essay three years earlier, is riddled with ____. Such phrases allow ugly realities to pass unexamined: when defenseless villages are bombed from the air, the operation is called pacification. The danger is not that words make thought impossible but that they can make careless or dishonest thinking easier.

Closed-circuit television cameras have become so ubiquitous in cities that most residents scarcely register them, and governments routinely justify new installations by pledging safer streets. ( ① ) The evidence for that pledge is more equivocal than the enthusiasm suggests. ( ② ) Large meta-analyses that aggregated decades of studies have found that cameras are associated with a modest reduction in crime overall, but the effect is clustered in particular settings, notably car parks and residential areas. ( ③ ) For violent offenses, which are often impulsive and committed in the heat of the moment, the deterrent effect appears negligible. ( ④ ) Cameras seem to work best when they are vigilantly monitored and combined with other measures, such as improved lighting or regular patrols. ( ⑤ ) Critics also warn of displacement, the possibility that offenders simply relocate to streets beyond the cameras' reach, though several studies suggest that nearby areas sometimes benefit instead. None of this means that cameras are futile; recorded footage frequently enables investigators to pinpoint suspects after the fact. But a camera that deters a calculating thief may mean nothing to a person in a paroxysm of rage.

In his Second Treatise of Government, published in 1689, John Locke set out to explain how anything could rightfully become private property in a world that God, he assumed, had bestowed on humanity in common. ( ① ) His answer was labor. ( ② ) Every person owns his own body, Locke reasoned, and therefore the work of his hands. ( ③ ) When someone gathers apples from a wild tree or tills an unclaimed field, he mingles his labor with what nature provided and thereby makes it his own. ( ④ ) Locke attached two conditions to such acquisition: one may take only as much as one can use before it spoils, and there must be enough, and as good, left for others. ( ⑤ ) The theory proved enormously influential, shaping later arguments for limited government and individual rights. It was also put to troubling uses. Colonists in North America invoked it to claim that land not cultivated in the European manner was effectively vacant and could be appropriated, disregarding the ways in which indigenous peoples had long used it. Locke's provisos, critics note, were quietly forgotten by those who found his central idea convenient.

In a classic 1973 study, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman posed a deceptively simple question to their participants: in a typical English text, is the letter K more likely to appear as the first letter of a word or as the third? ( ① ) Most respondents chose the first position. ( ② ) In fact, words with K in the third position, such as ask, make, and like, are considerably more common. ( ③ ) The researchers attributed the error to what they called the availability heuristic. ( ④ ) In this case, words beginning with K spring to mind far more readily than words with K buried inside them, so people mistake ease of recall for frequency. ( ⑤ ) The same bias distorts our judgments of risk. Dramatic causes of death, such as plane crashes, homicides, and shark attacks, receive extensive media coverage and are therefore vivid in memory, so people tend to overestimate them, while quieter killers such as diabetes and strokes are underestimated. Policymakers are not immune: a single memorable disaster can divert public spending toward rare dangers while more prevalent ones are neglected.

On an August evening in 1913, the roulette wheel at the casino in Monte Carlo landed on black again and again. As the streak lengthened, gamblers thronged around the table, staking ever larger sums on red in the conviction that a reversal was overdue. ( ① ) The ball fell on black twenty-six times in a row before red finally appeared, and by then many of the bettors had squandered fortunes. ( ② ) Their blunder now bears the name of the place: the gambler's fallacy, or the Monte Carlo fallacy. ( ③ ) It is the belief that past outcomes of independent random events alter the probability of future ones. ( ④ ) The wheel is devoid of memory; on every spin, the chance of red or black is exactly what it was before. ( ⑤ ) The fallacy is not confined to casinos. Parents who have had several sons sometimes feel that a daughter is now more likely, and investors sometimes sell a stock simply because it has risen for several days in succession. Researchers have even found traces of it in the decisions of judges and loan officers, who seem loath to issue too many identical rulings in a row, as if fairness required the results to alternate.

Under South Korean law, children younger than fourteen cannot be held criminally culpable for their actions. Those aged ten to thirteen who commit offenses, known as chokbeop sonyeon, are instead referred to juvenile courts, which may impose protective measures such as probation or placement in a juvenile institution.
(A) Opponents counter that the number of such cases is small, that children of that age are still developing the capacity to grasp the consequences of their acts, and that harsher punishment seldom deters impulsive behavior. Many argue that resources would be better allocated to early intervention, counseling, and support for beleaguered families.
(B) In recent years, however, a series of highly publicized cases involving serious violence by children near the age limit has provoked public outrage. Critics contend that today's children mature earlier than those of the past and that some exploit the law, knowing they cannot be prosecuted. In 2022 the Ministry of Justice proposed lowering the upper age from fourteen to thirteen.
(C) The dispute thus pits two legitimate concerns against each other: the public's demand for accountability and the conviction that children should be treated differently from adults. Whatever the threshold, most experts agree that what happens after a young offender is caught matters more than the precise age written into the statute.

In 1679 the English Parliament passed the Habeas Corpus Act, fortifying one of the oldest protections in the common law. The Latin phrase, meaning you shall have the body, refers to a court order directing a jailer to bring a prisoner before a judge.
(A) The principle crossed the Atlantic with English settlers, and the framers of the United States Constitution enshrined it, permitting its suspension only in cases of rebellion or invasion. That exception proved consequential: at the outbreak of the Civil War, President Lincoln suspended the writ in certain areas, provoking an acrimonious dispute over whether the president or Congress held that power.
(B) Similar controversies have recurred in later emergencies, whenever governments have claimed the right to hold suspects without trial. The persistence of these debates suggests that the old writ remains anything but an antiquarian curiosity; it is a test that every state claiming to respect liberty must face.
(C) The order sounds merely procedural, but its implications are profound. The jailer must justify the detention by showing a lawful reason for it, and if he cannot, the prisoner must be released. A ruler can no longer simply make dissenters vanish into a cell without explanation.

In February 2025 the computer scientist Andrej Karpathy coined the phrase vibe coding to describe a new way of building software. Instead of writing code line by line, the programmer describes what he wants in plain language, lets an artificial intelligence system generate the code, and accepts the result largely without reading it.
(A) The phrase spread with astonishing rapidity, and by the end of the year Collins Dictionary had named it its word of the year. Enthusiasts extolled the way it enabled people with no technical training to build simple apps and websites in an afternoon.
(B) The debate echoes earlier quarrels about calculators and spelling checkers. Each tool eventually found its place, but only after people learned which tasks could safely be delegated and which still required human judgment and expertise.
(C) Seasoned programmers were more ambivalent. Code that no one has read, they warned, can conceal security flaws and errors that surface only later, when they are far harder and more costly to rectify. Several observers suggested that the approach suits impromptu experiments but not software on which people's money or safety depends.

Every autumn, the retired schoolteacher Mr. Baek entered the village pumpkin contest, and every autumn he lost to his neighbor Mr. Do, whose pumpkins were invariably larger.
(A) Mr. Baek gaped at it for a long moment, then asked whether Mr. Do had been playing the violin all summer. "Of course not," his neighbor replied cheerfully. "I can't play a note. But I needed you to stop watering yours at dawn and start practicing instead."
(B) The following autumn, Mr. Baek's pumpkin was enormous, and the villagers were certain he would finally win. On the morning of the contest, however, Mr. Do arrived pushing a wheelbarrow that held a pumpkin so colossal it had cracked the barrow's wooden sides.
(C) One year, determined to discover the secret, Mr. Baek invited his rival to dinner and, over a third glass of rice wine, asked him point-blank. Mr. Do leaned forward conspiratorially and murmured that he played the violin to his pumpkins every evening. The next morning Mr. Baek bought a violin.

In 2008 South Korea introduced citizen participation trials, its first experiment with juries in criminal cases. Under the system, a defendant charged with a serious crime may request that ordinary citizens hear the evidence alongside professional judges. ① The jurors deliberate and deliver a verdict, but their decision is merely advisory: the judges are not legally bound to follow it. ② In practice, however, judges have agreed with the jury's verdict in the great majority of cases. ③ The Korean court system also includes specialized courts for family matters and for administrative disputes involving government agencies. ④ Supporters argue that the trials make the judiciary more transparent and bring the law closer to the people it serves. ⑤ Skeptics note that only a meager share of eligible defendants request them, partly because the process is unfamiliar and partly because some lawyers doubt that juries will be sympathetic. Proposals to make jury verdicts binding have been mooted repeatedly, but for now the system remains a cautious hybrid between the lay participation familiar in many countries and Korea's long tradition of trial by professional judges.

Teachers spend countless hours grading, on the assumption that marks motivate students and tell them how they are faring. A well-known study by the Israeli psychologist Ruth Butler, published in 1988, cast doubt on that assumption. ① Butler gave schoolchildren a series of thinking tasks and returned their work with one of three kinds of feedback: written comments alone, numerical grades alone, or comments together with grades. ② Students who received only comments displayed greater interest in the tasks and performed better in later sessions. ③ Numerical grading systems vary widely between countries, from letters in the United States to scales of twenty in France. ④ Strikingly, students who received both comments and grades fared no better than those who received grades alone. ⑤ The grade, it seems, eclipsed the comment: students glanced at the number, compared it with their classmates' scores, and ignored the advice beside it. Few schools can abandon grades entirely, but the study suggests that feedback intended to help students improve may be more potent when it is delivered before, or instead of, a mark.

Vampire bats live on a diet that leaves no margin for error. ① A common vampire bat must drink blood almost every night; after two or three nights without a meal, it may starve to death. ② Since roughly a third of young bats fail to find a meal on any given night, survival would seem to be largely a matter of luck. ③ In 1984, however, the biologist Gerald Wilkinson reported that bats returning to the roost with a full stomach often regurgitate blood to feed hungry roost-mates. ④ Bats are also the only mammals capable of true powered flight, and they account for roughly a fifth of all mammal species. ⑤ Crucially, the sharing is not indiscriminate: bats are more likely to feed individuals that have fed them in the past, as well as their close kin. Later experiments found that bats which had cultivated a wide network of sharing partners coped better when a regular partner was removed. The arrangement resembles a system of mutual insurance, and it has become one of the most frequently cited examples of reciprocal altruism among animals.

In 1377 the North African scholar Ibn Khaldun completed the Muqaddimah, an introduction to a history of the world that has since been hailed as a precursor of sociology. ① Dissatisfied with chroniclers who merely recorded events, he sought the underlying causes of the rise and fall of dynasties. ② His central concept was asabiyya, a form of group solidarity that he found strongest among the hardy peoples of the desert. ③ Bound by this cohesion, such groups could conquer settled kingdoms, but once established in cities, their descendants grew accustomed to luxury, their solidarity eroded, and they became prey to a new group from the margins. ④ Ibn Khaldun himself served several rulers as a judge and adviser and, late in life, met the conqueror Timur outside Damascus. ⑤ By his reckoning, the cycle typically ran its course within three or four generations. Modern historians question the regularity of the pattern, yet Ibn Khaldun's insistence that history should be explained by social forces rather than by the deeds of great men remains strikingly modern.

Vincent van Gogh wrote more than eight hundred letters that survive, most of them to his younger brother Theo, an art dealer in Paris who subsidized him for much of his adult life. They are vivid, erudite, and often harrowing, for Vincent describes the paintings he is working on, sketches them in the margins, argues about color and literature, and confesses his loneliness and fear of failure. Without them, the popular image of the artist would be far poorer. He sold scarcely any paintings during his lifetime, and when he died in 1890, followed by Theo only six months later, his reputation might easily have sunk into oblivion. That it did not is due in large part to Theo's widow, Johanna van Gogh-Bonger. She orchestrated exhibitions of Vincent's work, haggled with dealers, and spent years transcribing the letters, which she published in 1914. In her introduction she insisted that readers should come to know the man before judging the paintings. The strategy succeeded spectacularly: the letters transformed an obscure painter into one of the most beloved figures in the history of art, and they remain one of the most moving records of an artistic life ever written.

In November 2025, after two decades of planning, construction, and repeated delays, the Grand Egyptian Museum officially opened beside the pyramids of Giza. Touted as the largest museum in the world devoted to a single civilization, it houses tens of thousands of artifacts, including, for the first time in one place, the entire collection of objects found in the tomb of Tutankhamun. Visitors enter through a vast atrium dominated by a colossal statue of Ramesses II, which was moved to the site from central Cairo. Egyptian officials have presented the museum not only as a lure for tourism but as a statement of cultural sovereignty. For two centuries, many of the most celebrated Egyptian antiquities have been displayed in European and American museums, and Egyptian scholars have long argued that some of them should return. The new building bolsters their position. Museums abroad have often justified keeping such objects by contending that their countries of origin could not care for them adequately. A state-of-the-art institution beside the pyramids ____.

The Art of War, attributed to the Chinese general Sun Tzu and probably compiled around the fifth century BCE, is often imagined as a manual of ruthless aggression. Its central teaching is almost the opposite, for the supreme achievement, the text declares, is not to win a hundred battles but to subdue the enemy without fighting at all. Warfare is portrayed as ruinously expensive: it depletes treasuries, drains the population, and invites opportunistic neighbors to attack a weakened state. The wise commander therefore seeks to thwart the enemy's plans, sever his alliances, and prevail through deception, intelligence, and positioning before a single soldier is committed. Knowledge is paramount; a general who knows both the enemy and himself, the text famously asserts, need not fear the outcome of a hundred battles. Little wonder that executives, diplomats, and sports coaches have adopted the book as a guide. Read carefully, The Art of War is less a glorification of combat than an argument that the most skillful victory is ____.

Hotels have long placed cards in their bathrooms urging guests to reuse their towels in order to protect the environment. In a 2008 study, the psychologists Noah Goldstein, Robert Cialdini, and Vladas Griskevicius tested whether a subtle change in wording could make these appeals more persuasive. One version of the card offered the standard environmental message. Another informed guests that the majority of people staying in the hotel had reused their towels at least once. The second card increased reuse substantially, and a version noting that most previous guests who had stayed in that very room had done so proved more effective still. The finding illustrates the power of descriptive social norms: people look to the behavior of others, especially others in circumstances resembling their own, to gauge what is appropriate. It also carries a sobering warning for campaigners. Messages that lament how many people litter, squander water, or skip vaccinations may inadvertently ____, signaling that the undesirable behavior is perfectly normal.

The immune system confronts a perpetual dilemma: it must attack bacteria and viruses with ferocity, yet it must never turn that ferocity against the body's own tissues. For decades, scientists presumed that this restraint was achieved mainly in the thymus, where immune cells that react against the body are culled before they mature. The 2025 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine honored three researchers who showed that this is only part of the story. In 1995 the Japanese immunologist Shimon Sakaguchi identified a previously unknown class of cells, now called regulatory T cells, that patrol the body and suppress immune reactions that might otherwise damage healthy tissue. Several years later, the geneticists Mary Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell, studying a strain of mice prone to severe autoimmune disease, discovered a gene essential to these cells, and showed that mutations in the same gene cause a rare and serious disorder in humans. Their work revealed that the body's defense depends on ____. Researchers are now exploring ways to boost these cells to treat autoimmune diseases, or to weaken them so that the immune system can attack tumors more vigorously.

Many of the fables attributed to Aesop end with a tidy lesson: slow and steady wins the race, or it is easy to despise what you cannot get. Yet almost nothing certain is known about Aesop himself. Ancient chroniclers described him as a slave who lived on the Greek island of Samos in the sixth century BCE and won his freedom through his wit, but much of his biography is apocryphal. The fables circulated orally for centuries before they were written down, and the extant collections were assembled long after his death by compilers who interpolated, altered, and sometimes fabricated stories. Scholars have also noticed that the morals attached to the fables frequently sit incongruously with the stories themselves. The fox who dismisses the grapes as sour, for instance, can be read as a lesson in self-deception, in consolation, or in plain good sense, depending on the reader. The neat sentences at the end were often added by later editors eager to make the tales serve as edification. Read without those morals, the fables ____.

Every Sunday morning the laundromat on our corner held the same three customers: a nurse who slept through the whole cycle, a student with enormous headphones, and an elderly man in a pressed gray suit who worked the crossword in the newspaper. I was (A) [curious / incurious] about him for months before I mustered the courage to speak. One morning he sighed ruefully and tapped the page with his pen. Nine letters, he said, meaning stubborn, and he looked thoroughly vexed. I suggested obstinate, and he wrote it in with visible (B) [delight / reluctance]. After that, he saved the hardest clues for me. I learned that he had been a court interpreter for forty years and that he did the puzzle because his late wife had always done it with him; finishing it alone, he admitted, felt like an (C) [admission / denial] that she was really gone. So we finished it together, week after week, until the spring he moved to his daughter's city. He left an envelope with the attendant addressed to me. Inside was a dictionary, its margins crowded with his tiny handwriting, and a note that said only: for the next nine letters.

Teenagers who struggle to get out of bed are often accused of laziness, but biology offers a more charitable and plausible explanation. During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts later, so that many teenagers do not feel sleepy until well after eleven at night. Early school start times therefore (A) [deprive / provide] them of the sleep they need, with repercussions for attention, mood, and even road safety. In 2014 the American Academy of Pediatrics recommended that middle and high schools begin no earlier than 8:30 in the morning.
